title: The One In Vegas

jokes.text: No, it's just that all the people in the world I would want to talk to are right here.
jokes.setup: Monica asks Phoebe to get the phone, suggesting she's just being lazy.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reframes her laziness as a sentimental compliment to the group, delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe move — using sweetness as a shield for self-interest. The reframe works because it's both transparently lazy AND genuinely affectionate at once. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Can you answer the phone?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why? So you can avoid getting up off the couch?

jokes.text: I scratched it on the ATM machine on the corner.
jokes.setup: Joey calls asking for his PIN number because he forgot it, implying he stored it somewhere safe.
jokes.punchline: He scratched it directly onto the public ATM machine — the least secure location imaginable.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Joey joke because it's perfectly calibrated stupidity — not random dumb, but a logical-to-Joey solution that is catastrophically wrong. The structure is tight: setup implies a reasonable answer, punchline obliterates it. High character integration; only Joey would do this and feel good about it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not lazy! I just... I like to think of myself as 'energy efficient.'

jokes.text: Tribbiani, get back to work. Break time's over.
jokes.setup: Joey is on the phone talking about his big movie. The audience expects a movie star moment.
jokes.punchline: His 'stunt double' barks orders at him like a boss — immediately deflating the movie star image.
jokes.explanation: Smart piece of misdirection that plants the seed for the Vegas reveal. The stunt double bossing Joey around is a small but perfect comedic inversion of the star/double hierarchy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you're all gonna die soon and I'm gonna eat all your stuff.

jokes.text: Which Richard? Richard Simmons? Oh, my God!
jokes.setup: Monica says she ran into 'Richard' and can't tell Chandler.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's first assumption is Richard Simmons — the fitness personality — delivered with genuine excitement before the correction.
jokes.explanation: Quick misdirection gag that works on the absurdity of the assumption. Rachel's instant excitement about Richard Simmons is a good character beat — she'd genuinely love that.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't remember my PIN!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what did you do?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I scratched it into the ATM so I wouldn't forget it again.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey! That's your pin number! Anyone can see it now!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No they can't, I wrote it really small.

jokes.text: That's weird. I dreamed you had lunch with Richard. Again, Richard Simmons.
jokes.setup: Monica reveals the Richard lunch wasn't a big deal. Rachel makes an odd comment about dreaming the same thing.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately clarifies — again — that she means Richard Simmons, suggesting she thinks about him often enough to dream about him.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Simmons lands because Rachel doubles down immediately, the 'again' self-correction adding a layer — she knows she has this fixation. Good economy and timing implied by structure.

dialogue.speaker: Stunt Double
dialogue.line: Get back to work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Who do you think you are?

dialogue.speaker: Stunt Double
dialogue.line: I'm your stunt double.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, you can't talk to me like that!

dialogue.speaker: Stunt Double
dialogue.line: Actually, I can. I'm doubling for you.

jokes.text: I can't believe you guys have lasted a whole year! Wow, I owe Rachel 20 bucks. On a totally different bet.
jokes.setup: Phoebe sincerely congratulates Monica and Chandler on their anniversary, seemingly touched.
jokes.punchline: The aside about owing Rachel $20 implies she bet AGAINST the relationship, immediately deflating the sentiment — then the 'totally different bet' callback makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke that earns full marks for structure. The first beat (owing Rachel $20) undercuts Phoebe's warmth perfectly. The immediate 'totally different bet' correction is funnier than the original joke — implies there was a SECOND bet whose nature is now mysterious and presumably worse. Tight, well-constructed, very Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what, random people just come up to you asking for pictures?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, it happens all the time now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? Where?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It was Entertainment Tonight.

jokes.text: Now you're just my annoying friend Chandler.
jokes.setup: Chandler romanticizes their anniversary, saying a year ago he was 'just her annoying friend Chandler.'
jokes.punchline: Monica confirms that description hasn't changed — undercutting his nostalgia with affectionate dismissal.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — Monica takes Chandler's own framing and flips it back on him in four words. The affection underneath makes it land warmly rather than cruelly. Classic sitcom couple banter.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, you ran into Richard? Richard Simmons?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, not Richard Simmons. Richard Burke. My ex-boyfriend.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you ran into him? Where? What did he say?

jokes.text: We can call it our 'Plane-aversary.'
jokes.setup: Chandler excitedly explains they'll start celebrating their anniversary on the plane.
jokes.punchline: He coins 'Plane-aversary' — an enthusiastic but terrible portmanteau that he seems proud of.
jokes.explanation: Setup for a running gag. The joke itself is mild — a bad portmanteau — but it's intentionally bad as character comedy for Chandler's over-eager romanticism.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, it's Richard Burke, not Richard Simmons!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, that makes so much more sense.

jokes.text: Do we have to?
jokes.setup: Chandler unveils 'Plane-aversary' with evident pride.
jokes.punchline: Monica's flat 'Do we have to?' is the audience surrogate reaction — perfectly timed deflation.
jokes.explanation: The straight-man response is funnier than the pun itself. Monica's weary three words carry perfect comic timing implied by the script. Good partnership dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I had this dream about Monica and Richard.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Richard? My Richard?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I'm still thinking about Richard Simmons.

jokes.text: 'Anna-Vegas-ry!' / 'Anna-vada-versary!'
jokes.setup: Having established 'Plane-aversary,' Chandler keeps trying to coin an anniversary portmanteau for Vegas.
jokes.punchline: Each attempt is worse than the last, escalating in absurdity with 'Anna-vada-versary' as the nadir.
jokes.explanation: The escalating badness of Chandler's portmanteau attempts is a good running gag. 'Anna-vada-versary' is impressively bad in a satisfying way. Character-specific to Chandler's coping-through-humor personality.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So you guys are actually staying together?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh thank God, because I have twenty bucks riding on you two breaking up.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean... not because I want you to break up. I just... I bet Joey that you wouldn't last.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How long?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A month.

jokes.text: I think we should see other people.
jokes.setup: Chandler lands 'Anna-vada-versary' as his worst attempt yet.
jokes.punchline: Monica responds as if breaking up with him, treating the bad wordplay as a relationship-ending offense.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the portmanteau gag. Monica's mock-breakup framing is proportionally absurd to the crime of bad wordplay. Economy is excellent — four words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Happy anniversary. I got you something special.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you didn't have to do that! But since you did, I hope you kept the receipt.

jokes.text: Phoebe, it's kind of our anniversary. / You won't ditch me like you did with London. Ditch you? You were pregnant. Great story. I'm going.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler gently try to point out this is their couples trip.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe steamrolls their objection by calling Monica's pregnancy a 'great story' — dismissing it as an excuse — and declaring she's going anyway.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe at her most delightfully self-centered. 'Ditch you? You were pregnant. Great story. I'm going.' is a rapid-fire dismissal that earns laughs through sheer audacity. Strong character integration — Phoebe's blithe obliviousness is perfectly rendered.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're celebrating our anniversary on a plane. It's very romantic. We're in the air, we're in love... we're... we're in-love!

jokes.text: Art lover.
jokes.setup: Ross says he can't go to Vegas because he has tickets to the Van Gogh exhibit he's waited a year for.
jokes.punchline: Someone (inferred from context, likely another friend) mutters 'art lover' as a mild, almost confused insult that doesn't quite land as an insult — which is what makes it funny.
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke here is that 'art lover' is barely an insult, and the follow-up 'Was that supposed to be an insult? I don't know, I'm very tired' makes explicit that the joke IS the failed insult. Self-aware and charming.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No. Absolutely not. We are not calling it that.

jokes.text: Was that supposed to be an insult? / I don't know, I'm very tired.
jokes.setup: 'Art lover' is muttered as a putdown.
jokes.punchline: The insulter admits they don't know if it was an insult, blaming tiredness — undercutting any comedic aggression with total self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The punchline being an admission that the punchline didn't work is a nice meta move. 'I'm very tired' as an excuse is very funny in its honesty. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Vegas? More like... Vegass. With an extra S. For... super.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Or Veg-ASS. You know, 'cause it's in the desert.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Veg-NASTY? No wait—Veg-ASS-ity.

jokes.text: To walk around naked.
jokes.setup: Ross says having the apartment to himself will be nice for 'alone time.'
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately and enthusiastically finishes the thought — 'To walk around naked' — as the obvious conclusion.
jokes.explanation: Joey's assumption that all alone-time is naked-time is a great character beat. It plants the seed for the later Rachel-window subplot. Perfect economy and high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I got you a present for our anniversary. I hope it's not a letdown... unlike our relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, if you make one more pun, I'm going to kill you in your sleep.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wow, that's a bit of an overreaction. I was just trying to have some fun... anniversary fun, get it?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's it. I'm done. I'm taking the apartment, the furniture, the dog we don't have, and I'm moving to Yemen.

jokes.text: Naked alone time.
jokes.setup: Ross protests that being alone doesn't mean walking around naked.
jokes.punchline: Joey repackages the concept as 'naked alone time' — a phrase that implies it's so normal it has its own compound noun.
jokes.explanation: The invention of 'naked alone time' as a recognized category of activity is good Joey logic. Brief but adds to the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You ditched me!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I didn't ditch you. I had to work late.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's what ditchers say.

jokes.text: You live alone, you don't walk around naked. Why does it take me so long to answer the door?
jokes.setup: Ross insists he doesn't walk around naked in his own apartment.
jokes.punchline: He immediately contradicts himself by wondering aloud why it takes him so long to answer the door — implying he has to get dressed first.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Ross vehemently denies Joey's claim, then inadvertently proves it correct in the same breath. The gap between assertion and self-incriminating question is perfectly constructed — the audience realizes what he's admitted before Ross does. Excellent structure, good economy, and the self-own is entirely earned.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Van Gogh? Please. The man cut off his own ear. I mean, what kind of artist does that?

jokes.text: What about after I give you these candies? / I guess it's a little better now. Las Vegas 1, London 0.
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks if Vegas is better than London so far, is told it's about the same.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe produces candy to tip the scales, and Monica concedes one point to Vegas — Phoebe treating this like a formal competition with a running score.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's scorecard conceit is a fun character beat. Using candy as the decisive factor in a London vs. Vegas comparison is Phoebe's very specific brand of logic.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What was that supposed to mean?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Nothing, I just... you know what, never mind.

jokes.text: Oh, don't tell me I did this. / I love the 'I forgot the present' fake-out!
jokes.setup: Chandler reaches for Monica's anniversary gift and appears to realize he forgot it.
jokes.punchline: Monica assumes it's a fake-out game she loves — but Chandler confirms he genuinely forgot.
jokes.explanation: Good two-beat structure — Monica's delighted 'I love this fake-out' makes Chandler's correction ('it's not a fake-out') land harder. The audience's expectation is shaped by Monica's expectation, then both are defeated.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I just want some time alone, you know? For solitude and quiet reflection.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Plus I can walk around naked.

jokes.text: You decided to tell him about the Richard thing.
jokes.setup: Chandler says forgetting the gift is the worst thing that could happen.
jokes.punchline: Rachel, thinking aloud, assumes Monica has told Chandler about the secret Richard lunch — inadvertently outing the secret in front of Chandler.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom dramatic irony executed well. The setup (Chandler lamenting the worst thing) + Rachel's assumption creates a perfect accidental reveal. The 'Oh no' that follows is earned. Well-structured farce moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't just walk around naked when I'm alone.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, you do.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, I don't!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Dude, I've seen you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, that doesn't... I mean, that was one time!

jokes.text: Simmons. Go with Simmons.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks 'What Richard thing?' and Monica panics.
jokes.punchline: Rachel desperately whispers her cover story suggestion — Richard Simmons — as damage control, calling back the earlier confusion.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed callback. 'Simmons. Go with Simmons.' is a great line — urgent, ridiculous, and referencing the earlier running joke. The economy is excellent; three words do complete comic work.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I got candy on the plane! This is so exciting! I'm keeping score between trips now.

jokes.text: So you bumped into Richard. You grabbed a 'bite.' No big deal.
jokes.setup: Monica explains the innocent lunch with Richard. Chandler says he's not mad.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's air-quotes around 'bite' and his tightly controlled 'no big deal' — punctuated by increasingly long pauses — reveal he is absolutely not fine.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's suppressed jealousy played through clipped, over-controlled sentences is good cringe comedy. The pauses noted in the transcript (08:18, 08:23) make clear this is uncomfortable silence used as a comedic beat. Strong character integration — Chandler's anxiety masked by false calm is a core character trait.

jokes.text: Okay, London 1. This is gonna be a real horserace.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler's argument makes the Vegas trip tense.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe updates the London vs. Vegas scoreboard after the Richard revelation sours the trip, treating relationship drama as a point in London's favor.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff. Phoebe treating Monica's relationship meltdown as a data point in her travel comparison is blissfully oblivious and perfectly in character. 'Real horserace' is a funny phrase to use about a one-all scoreline.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I actually forgot your birthday present!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? You forgot?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm sorry. I got you something, but then I realized it was stupid, so I returned it. And then I forgot to get you something else.

jokes.text: I'm lighting the candles. Naked. And carefully.
jokes.setup: Ross is gleefully narrating his naked apartment experience.
jokes.punchline: 'And carefully' — the addition of this word implies the specific physical peril of naked candle-lighting, which the audience's imagination fills in.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'And carefully' is the perfect button — two words that force the audience to imagine exactly why candle-lighting naked requires care. The understatement does enormous work. Economy is near-perfect: nine words total in the setup, two words deliver the laugh. High quotability. This is exactly what good economy looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what's the deal with you and Richard?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh! Richard Simmons! Have you seen him lately? He's got amazing energy!

jokes.text: Oh, my God! That's Rachel, naked!
jokes.setup: Ross is happily naked in his apartment when he notices something across the way.
jokes.punchline: He sees Rachel naked in her apartment window — the joke is the collision of his own nakedness with hers, and his panicked reaction.
jokes.explanation: The setup of the whole naked subplot pays off with this visual reveal. Standard sitcom farce construction but executed cleanly. The audience has been primed to find this funny by the earlier naked narration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, so Monica and Chandler had a fight on the plane, which means... Joey and I are still tied.

jokes.text: I can't look at that. I am looking at this. Okay, vivid colors, expressive brush strokes.
jokes.setup: Ross spots Rachel naked through the window and forces himself to look away.
jokes.punchline: He immediately contradicts 'I can't look' with 'I am looking' — then pivots to art-criticism of the Van Gogh print on his wall as self-distraction, mentioning the same exhibit he stayed home for.
jokes.explanation: Ross's rationalization spiral — 'can't look / am looking / okay Van Gogh' — is a good character beat. The callback to the Van Gogh exhibit (why he stayed home) adds an ironic layer. His self-narration voice returns from the naked candle scene.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And here we see the male of the species in his natural habitat, completely unclothed and vulnerable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: He approaches the refrigerator, searching for sustenance, unaware that he is being observed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Notice how he carefully adjusts the thermostat, ensuring optimal comfort for his exposed skin.

jokes.text: She knows I'm home. She knows I can see her. What kind of game is she playing? I think maybe someone's lonely tonight.
jokes.setup: Ross spots Rachel naked through the window and begins to rationalize what he sees.
jokes.punchline: Ross's internal logic escalates from observation to full romantic misreading — he concludes she's lonely and interested, entirely on his own projection.
jokes.explanation: Ross's self-delusion engine running at full speed. The progression from 'she can see me' to 'she's lonely' in four sentences is perfect Ross — his ability to construct elaborate romantic narratives from almost nothing is a core character trait.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, this is nice. Just me, completely naked, no one around...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait... is that... Rachel?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

jokes.text: I wanna lay down a couple of ground rules. This is just about tonight. I won't go through with this if it'll raise the question of 'us.'
jokes.setup: Ross goes to Rachel's door after completely misreading her nakedness. He believes she's been signaling romantic interest.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately launches into ground rules for a hookup that Rachel has not agreed to, never proposed, and is about to be horrified by.
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe comedy — the audience knows Ross has catastrophically misread the situation, and watching him double down with 'ground rules' for a scenario that doesn't exist is painfully funny. His self-importance ('I won't go through with this if...') adds to the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She wanted me to see her. She definitely wanted me to see her. Why else would she be naked? She was sending me a signal. A very clear, very naked signal.

jokes.text: And... what is that, Ross? / The physical act of love.
jokes.setup: Ross has been setting ground rules for 'what this is.'
jokes.punchline: When Rachel asks him to define 'it,' Ross delivers 'the physical act of love' — a hilariously clinical, formal euphemism that reveals both his anxiety and his obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: Excellent delivery vehicle for Ross's character. 'The physical act of love' is perfectly calibrated awkward-academic language — the kind of phrase a paleontologist might use. The formality is funnier than any crude alternative would be. High quotability and strong character integration. The pause implied before Rachel's incredulous 'What, are you crazy?' sells it further.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, it would be a fascinating encounter from a paleontological perspective. We could discuss the evolutionary advantages of bipedalism, perhaps examine some fossilized remains, and engage in a rigorous academic dialogue about Mesozoic extinction events.

jokes.text: What, are you crazy? So you weren't trying to entice me just now with your nakedness?
jokes.setup: Ross lays out ground rules for their 'hookup.'
jokes.punchline: Rachel's reality check ('What, are you crazy?') followed by Ross doubling down — genuinely asking if she was trying to entice him — escalates the cringe to its peak.
jokes.explanation: The cringe peaks when Ross, even after being called crazy, holds his ground by asking if she was 'trying to entice him with her nakedness.' His persistence in the face of obvious rejection is painfully perfect Ross-behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, so all that 'evidence' of him trying to seduce me was just... him removing his shoes?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I was getting comfortable!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You literally spent twenty minutes explaining how taking off your footwear was a classic seduction technique.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, it's in the Paleontology Manual of Dating!

jokes.text: Oh, wow. I'm sorry. But, Ross, you kicked off your shoes.
jokes.setup: Ross is mortified after the full misunderstanding is revealed.
jokes.punchline: Rachel, trying to be empathetic, notes that he 'kicked off his shoes' — implying he got that far into preparing for a hookup — which makes it somehow worse.
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of 'you kicked off your shoes' is perfect — it's specific enough to be visual, embarrassing enough to deepen Ross's humiliation, and 'you kicked off your shoes' has become a shorthand for getting ahead of oneself. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, if the price was right, I'd eat people.

jokes.text: Do we still need to settle the question of 'us'?
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel agree to never mention the incident again.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately breaks the truce by asking if they still need to address their relationship — unable to let it go even after total humiliation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character button. Ross agrees to drop it, then immediately doesn't. 'One more thing' followed by the callback to his own ground rules speech is very Ross — his inability to let the Ross/Rachel question go even at the worst possible moment is true to character.

jokes.text: For ninety-nine cents I'd eat you.
jokes.setup: Phoebe notes the steak and lobster dinner special, and someone points out she doesn't eat animals.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe casually announces she'd cannibalize her companion for 99 cents — a cheerful threat that's both dark and completely Phoebe.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's cheerful cannibalism threat is a perfect expression of her character — the childlike sweetness masking something faintly unhinged. 'For ninety-nine cents I'd eat you' works on multiple levels: it's a price-rationalization joke, a character joke, and a dark joke all at once. Economy is excellent, quotability is high.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, Richard? He's so sophisticated and mature.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, he sounds like a game show host.

jokes.text: Love your condoms, my man.
jokes.setup: The group spots Joey in his casino gladiator costume.
jokes.punchline: Chandler greets him by complimenting his 'condoms' — the gladiator's decorative armor pieces — in a deliberately anachronistic/misidentified way.
jokes.explanation: Quick visual gag — Chandler misidentifying the decorative armor as something else. Light laugh, good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry, did my hair get in the way of your career?

jokes.text: Why are you dressed as a gladiator? / Because I'm shooting a scene right now. I play a gladiator.
jokes.setup: Joey's friends see him in a gladiator costume at a casino.
jokes.punchline: Joey defends it as being for his movie — which sets up the reveal that the movie no longer exists.
jokes.explanation: Setup beat for the larger reveal. Functional but not particularly funny on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's not that bad. I mean, so what if a few people saw you naked?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A few people?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. The whole building saw you naked.

jokes.text: Hold on a second. Can we cut? My friends are here. I'm gonna take a break. / Who are you talking to? The director. / Her.
jokes.setup: Joey calls for a cut to take a break, naming 'the director.'
jokes.punchline: The director is a random casino patron — presumably a pit boss or showgirl — making Joey's professional pretense collapse immediately.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of 'the director' as a random casino employee is a good visual punchline. 'Her.' is a perfect minimalist button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't embarrass easily.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh really? ROSS! ROSS! Everyone, this is my friend Ross. He's never been with a woman!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel!

jokes.text: All right, it's not a gladiator movie. I work here.
jokes.setup: Joey has been maintaining movie star pretense. His friends press him.
jokes.punchline: The full reveal: Joey is a casino gladiator greeter, not a movie actor. The deflation of the entire premise lands here.
jokes.explanation: The long-awaited reveal pays off the cold open hints. Joey's admission is played with resigned dignity, which is funnier than embarrassment would be.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: If I won the lottery, I'd have an elaborate scheme to assault Richard.

jokes.text: Monica had lunch with Richard. / Dawson? But that would've been so cool!
jokes.setup: Chandler reveals Monica had a secret lunch with Richard.
jokes.punchline: Joey assumes Richard Dawson (Family Feud host) — expressing genuine disappointment it was Monica's ex instead.
jokes.explanation: Extends the 'wrong Richard' running gag but subverts it differently — this time it's Joey jumping to Richard Dawson rather than Richard Simmons. His genuine disappointment ('That would've been so cool!') is very Joey. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we're going to Vegas! We're going to Vegas! We're going to Vegas!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm gonna wear a low-cut top and have a fake ID that says I'm a cocktail waitress!

jokes.text: When you go lunching with hunky men and don't tell me!
jokes.setup: Monica challenges Chandler's trust issues. He explains what upset him.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's complaint focuses on 'hunky' as his descriptor for Richard — a word choice that reveals both his insecurity and his slightly melodramatic vocabulary.
jokes.explanation: The word 'hunky' coming from Chandler is unexpected and funny — his insecurity expressing itself in slightly flamboyant language is very true to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. I just realized something. We could be hand twins!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hand twins?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah! You know, like identical twins, but just for hands. We could go on talk shows and be like, 'Look at our identical hands!'

jokes.text: 'Next time'? / So close.
jokes.setup: Monica, trying to make peace, says she'll tell Chandler next time she sees Richard.
jokes.punchline: Chandler catches the implied 'next time' — there's apparently going to be one — and Joey, as an observer, mutters 'So close' as Monica nearly resolved things then immediately unresolved them.
jokes.explanation: Joey's bystander commentary 'So close' is perfectly timed and very funny. The structure — Monica's inadvertent mistake, Chandler catching it, Joey narrating the disaster — is tight and well-executed. 'So close' as a reaction beat carries the whole joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look at this! Our hands are identical!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, we're not identical twins. You have your hands, I have mine. They just... look like hands.

jokes.text: That's funny, I think I just did.
jokes.setup: Monica tells Chandler he can't tell her what to do.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's flat 'That's funny, I think I just did' — delivered as a rare moment of confident Chandler.
jokes.explanation: Good economy. Chandler's rare assertiveness is funnier precisely because he's usually a pushover. The deadpan line reading implied is very Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, so here's the thing. I've got this amazing business opportunity. You pay me fifty bucks, and I show you my hands. Then I show you my hands again. Identical! Same hands! How'd I do it?

jokes.text: Don't look at me. I just work here.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are having a full argument in the middle of the casino floor while Joey stands between them in a gladiator costume.
jokes.punchline: Joey disavows involvement with a casino-employee disclaimer that's simultaneously true (he does work there) and absurd (he's also their friend).
jokes.explanation: Perfect use of the gladiator-job reveal. The line works on two levels: Joey deflecting from friend-drama, AND Joey genuinely being a casino employee for once playing a neutral party. The costume makes the line funnier than it would otherwise be. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's amazing! You have a hand twin? That's like... that's like finding your soulmate, but for hands!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You guys, this is so romantic. I'm getting emotional.

jokes.text: Ross? I'm a little warm, so I'm gonna be taking off my sweater. Now, I'm just letting you know... this is not an invitation to the physical act of love.
jokes.setup: Rachel and Ross are on the plane together after the nakedness misunderstanding.
jokes.punchline: Rachel formally announces her sweater removal is not a sexual invitation — using Ross's exact phrase 'the physical act of love' as a callback weapon.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. Rachel weaponizes Ross's own absurd terminology back at him — 'the physical act of love' — deployed with perfect comic control. The callback lands exponentially harder because it uses his exact pompous language. The structure is excellent: the sweater setup mimics the original nakedness misunderstanding, then 'this is not an invitation to the physical act of love' is both a payoff and a humiliation. High quotability, strong character integration, and the best laugh of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You look like Pancho Villa!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I do not look like Pancho Villa.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, you do a little bit.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And Rachel looks like Vanna White!

jokes.text: Yep, that's hilarious. I'm sorry. I'm done. I'm done.
jokes.setup: Rachel delivers the callback line about the physical act of love.
jokes.punchline: Ross's attempt to dismiss it with 'that's hilarious' fails as he cracks and admits he's embarrassed, repeating 'I'm done' — the stammer revealing his mortification.
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — Ross's failed 'I'm fine' followed by collapsing into genuine embarrassment ('I'm done. I'm done.') is true to character and extends the joke a beat further.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm taking dance karate. It's like a beautiful blend of movement and self-defense. You leap through the air, and you're also kicking people.

jokes.text: No, not really. You've seen me naked hundreds of times. But it was a first for the rest of my building.
jokes.setup: Ross says the nakedness incident must have been embarrassing for Rachel too.
jokes.punchline: Rachel confirms Ross isn't special for seeing her naked — but then reveals she was visible to her entire apartment building.
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke with a great escalation. The first beat ('you've seen me naked hundreds of times') reframes the incident as normal for Ross; the second beat ('first for the rest of my building') reveals the actual scope of her exposure. Well-structured, the escalation is earned.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A hand twin! Do you know how rare that is? We could do everything together! We could be hand models, we could open a hand modeling agency, we could have a mansion with a hand-shaped pool, and a hand-shaped hot tub, and little hand-shaped guest houses!

jokes.text: Hey, lady! I don't care how much you want it, okay? I am not gonna have sex with you in the bathroom!
jokes.setup: Rachel has been ribbing Ross about his self-proclaimed emotional security.
jokes.punchline: Ross — trying to prove his confidence by talking to a stranger — shouts a loudly non-consensual rejection at a random woman, exposing his compensating bravado.
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy implied by the structure — Ross trying to demonstrate confidence ends in spectacular miscalculation. The specificity of 'in the bathroom' makes it funnier. Proves Rachel's point immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What did the hotel person say about the permanent marker?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: The only takeaway was a personal compliment.

jokes.text: You know, in Roman times, this was more than just a hat...
jokes.setup: Joey is in his gladiator costume greeting casino guests and trying to make conversation.
jokes.punchline: Joey begins a probably-wrong historical explanation of his helmet, segueing into increasingly ridiculous uses (scrubbing floors, cleaning horses) — clearly making it up.
jokes.explanation: Joey's confident-but-wrong historical improvisation is in character. The escalating uses of the helmet as domestic tool is absurdist and reveals Joey trying very hard to seem knowledgeable while clearly having no idea.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! There's a face drawn all over my face!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, yeah. We were trying to cheer you up.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: By drawing a face on my face?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's the smiley face. You know, to make you smile.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, it's not working!

jokes.text: If I won $5000, I'd join a gym. Build up my upper body... and hit Richard from behind with a stick.
jokes.setup: Chandler hears that a blackjack player won $5000 and muses what he'd do with the money.
jokes.punchline: What begins as a reasonable statement about gym membership escalates into a plan to physically assault Richard — Chandler processing his jealousy through fantasy violence.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. The structure is excellent: 'join a gym / build my upper body' sets up something reasonable, then the punchline pivots hard to 'hit Richard from behind with a stick.' The specificity of 'from behind' (cowardly but strategic) is a great detail. Very high character integration — this is Chandler's jealousy, self-deprecation, and dark humor all at once. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know, it's not fair how you're treating her like a criminal just because she's winning.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She's been playing the same machine for six hours straight.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So? Maybe she's just really committed to it. That doesn't make her a bad person.

jokes.text: Good luck. / I don't need luck. I've thought this through. / I see.
jokes.setup: Joey announces he's going to gamble $100 to revive his movie.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'I see' in response to 'I've thought this through' is pure deadpan — implying exactly the opposite of what Joey claims.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's two-word 'I see' carries perfect skepticism. Economy is near-perfect — he conveys complete disbelief in two syllables. Good straight-man work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: 🎵 You're my hand twin, my hand twin, we look so much alike. You're my hand twin, my hand twin, I like you, I really like you. But which one are you? Are you the left or right? I can never tell, I can never tell, you're driving me crazy tonight! 🎵

jokes.text: Big deal. It's only Chandler.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is comforting Monica about her fight with Chandler.
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a genuinely sympathetic moment, Phoebe diminishes Chandler to 'it's only Chandler' — accidentally harsh, entirely Phoebe.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's oblivious minimizing of Chandler is funny because it comes from genuine comfort-giving — she doesn't mean to be dismissive. 'It's only Chandler' as a reassurance is both sweet and terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going to roll the dice. If I get a seven, I'm proposing to Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?! Chandler, you can't base a marriage proposal on a dice roll!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why not? It's worked for everything else in my life.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, it hasn't!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, you're right. But I'm doing it anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Here goes... *rolls dice* Seven!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

jokes.text: Yeah! Las Vegas! Number one!
jokes.setup: Monica takes Phoebe's advice to go find Chandler and make up.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately switches from supportive friend to Vegas booster, updating her scorecard — the moment Monica leaves, the London vs. Vegas competition resumes.
jokes.explanation: Running gag continues. Phoebe's instant pivot from emotional support to Vegas cheerleading reveals her priorities, which is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm going to follow you everywhere you go.

dialogue.speaker: Old Lady
dialogue.line: Well, you could just take the bus with me.

jokes.text: Do you have any extra pants? My friend seems to have had a little accident.
jokes.setup: Ross's interaction with the stranger has apparently gone wrong in a physical way.
jokes.punchline: Rachel asks for 'extra pants' on Ross's behalf, her clinical understatement ('a little accident') making the humiliation more complete.
jokes.explanation: Rachel's matter-of-fact pants request is a good deadpan moment. 'A little accident' as a descriptor for whatever happened to Ross is perfectly understated.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: He stole my lucky harmonica in 1987!

jokes.text: Wait! You are not gonna believe this! I have found my identical hand twin.
jokes.setup: Joey was supposed to be gambling to save his movie. He returns with news.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a gambling update, Joey announces the discovery of his 'identical hand twin' — a concept he treats with the gravity of a scientific breakthrough.
jokes.explanation: 'Identical hand twin' is an inspired piece of Joey-absurdist logic. The concept is specific enough to be memorable and ridiculous enough to be funny on its own. Joey's breathless announcement treats this as the most important event of his life. Highly quotable phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I need a fake name and a new identity.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'll be Regina Phalange, and I'm a... licensed masseuse and massage therapist.

jokes.text: It was incredible. The dealer's hands were exactly like mine. It was like looking at my hands in a mirror!
jokes.setup: Joey explains the identical hand twin concept.
jokes.punchline: The mirror description — escalating his awe — is funny because it describes... what a mirror does, which is not special.
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-defeating analogy ('like looking at my hands in a mirror') inadvertently explains why this isn't amazing, without him noticing. Good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dealer
dialogue.line: Joey, I appreciate the enthusiasm, but 'hand twin' is not a viable business model.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But my hands are perfect! Look at them!

dialogue.speaker: Dealer
dialogue.line: I don't care if your hands cure cancer. If you don't stop pitching this, I'm going to break both of them and feed them to my dog.

jokes.text: You sure you weren't looking at your hands in a mirror?
jokes.setup: Joey says seeing the hand twin was 'like looking at his hands in a mirror.'
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks if Joey literally was just looking in a mirror — taking the bad analogy literally as a logical alternative.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's question perfectly exposes the logical gap in Joey's analogy. The economy is excellent — one sentence dismantles the whole hand twin premise while getting a big laugh. Classic straight-man work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Mrs. Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not Mrs. Ross. I'm Monica Geller.

jokes.text: I don't have it all worked out yet. But it's gotta mean big money.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks how identical hands will make Joey a millionaire.
jokes.punchline: Joey admits he has no idea how, but insists the money is inevitable — the confidence entirely unsupported by the plan.
jokes.explanation: Joey's confidence in an entirely unformed plan is a core character trait. 'I don't have it all worked out yet' as a response to 'how?' is perfect Joey logic.

jokes.text: This is Vegas, man. People will pay to see freaky stuff! How much would you pay to see this hand... twice?
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to explain the financial logic of the hand twin.
jokes.punchline: His pitch — 'how much would you pay to see this hand... twice?' — is delivered with utter sincerity, holding up his hand for emphasis.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Joey jokes. 'How much would you pay to see this hand... twice?' is an almost perfectly constructed absurdist pitch. The pause before 'twice,' the seriousness with which it's delivered, and the complete failure to explain why duplicate hands have entertainment value all combine beautifully. High character integration — only Joey could make this pitch with zero irony. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I can't really put a price on that. / Are you un-supporting me again?
jokes.setup: Joey asks how much Chandler would pay to see his hand twice.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's carefully hedged non-answer ('I can't really put a price on that') is immediately misread by Joey as hostility — 'Are you un-supporting me again?'
jokes.explanation: Chandler's diplomatic non-answer is funny, and Joey's jump to 'are you un-supporting me again?' callbacks the cold open perfectly. 'Un-supporting' as a verb is a good Joey coinage.

jokes.text: I gotta document this before that dealer gets off his break.
jokes.setup: Joey is planning the hand twin enterprise.
jokes.punchline: Joey's urgency to 'document' identical hands — and the implied bureaucracy of hand documentation — is an absurd detail that reveals he's taken this fully seriously.
jokes.explanation: Light gag but adds to the hand twin episode's absurdist escalation. 'Before the dealer gets off his break' adds some urgency to the ridiculous premise.

jokes.text: I found my identical hand twin! / Oh, you're so lucky!
jokes.setup: Joey shows Phoebe his hand and announces the hand twin.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe — the one person more credulous than Joey — responds with immediate sincere enthusiasm, validating the entire ludicrous concept.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character pairing. Phoebe is exactly the person who would call having an identical hand twin 'lucky' without any irony. The mutual validation between the show's two most credulous characters is very funny and highly character-specific.

jokes.text: She's probably talking to Richard. / Would you stop that? / You know what she said after her lunch with Richard? She didn't feel anything for him. She loves you.
jokes.setup: Chandler is brooding about Monica's absence, worried she's with Richard.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately fuels Chandler's paranoia by suggesting Monica is with Richard — before Rachel has to do damage control. Ross's obliviousness to making things worse is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Ross stirring the pot unintentionally is in character but not a particularly crafted joke. Functional narrative beat with mild comedy.

jokes.text: I should really start wearing hats.
jokes.setup: Ross's physical ordeal in the casino (pants incident, stranger encounter) has apparently been partly visible.
jokes.punchline: Ross's non-sequitur conclusion — that hats are the solution to his problems — is absurdist and reveals his fractured state of mind.
jokes.explanation: A quiet, odd little joke. 'I should really start wearing hats' as a reaction to a humiliating casino evening is a great non-sequitur. The connection between his ordeal and hats is unclear, which is what makes it funny.

jokes.text: Let me guess. Pancho Villa. / And you're Bob Saget.
jokes.setup: Phoebe arrives to find Ross and Rachel have drawn facial hair on each other.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe identifies Ross's drawn-on mustache as 'Pancho Villa,' then looks at Rachel and guesses 'Bob Saget' — the incongruity of the two celebrity comparisons being the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag. The pairing of Pancho Villa and Bob Saget is an unlikely combo that reveals what the drawn-on facial hair looks like. Phoebe's confident wrong-but-specific guesses work for her character.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! You drew on me? / Hey, you wet my pants! / What kind of party was this?
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are discovered to have drawn on each other's faces.
jokes.punchline: The escalating revelations — Rachel drew on Ross's face; he wet her pants — with Phoebe's confused 'what kind of party was this?' is the confused bystander reaction.
jokes.explanation: The mutual-destruction escalation is fun. Phoebe's bystander confusion ('what kind of party was this?') is a good button that recontextualizes the chaos from outside.

jokes.text: I bet she's one of those people. / Mole people? / What? No, a lurker.
jokes.setup: Chandler notices a woman keeps winning on machines he was just playing.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's first guess is 'mole people' — an absurd non-answer that she treats as a reasonable category of casino threat.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's jump to 'mole people' is a perfect absurdist Phoebe answer. It's specific enough to feel like she's genuinely considered underground casino-dwelling people as a threat, and 'What? No' from Chandler is the right straight-man response.

jokes.text: My nana used to do it. That's how she paid for my dance karate lessons. / Dance karate? / Yes, it's a deadly... but beautiful sport.
jokes.setup: Chandler explains what a 'lurker' is. Phoebe recognizes the concept.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's grandmother was a slot machine lurker — funding Phoebe's 'dance karate lessons.' The invention of 'dance karate' as its own discipline, described as 'deadly... but beautiful,' is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Dance karate' is an inspired invention — a perfect Phoebe concept that combines two things in a way that makes no sense but feels completely plausible for her backstory. The delivery of 'deadly... but beautiful sport' is exactly how Phoebe would describe it, with the pause making it funnier. Nana funding it through slot-lurking is an extra layer of absurd character history. Very high originality and character integration. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: I took it off and then I drew it back on.
jokes.setup: Rachel discovers facial hair drawn on her and is horrified. Ross says he thinks it'll come off.
jokes.punchline: Ross's admission that he initially removed the beard... then redrew it on Rachel's face — compounding the crime and revealing he made a deliberate choice.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup implies they were both victimized — Ross drew on Rachel and she drew on him. The punchline reveals Ross thought about removing the beard from Rachel's face, took it off, then PUT IT BACK. This deliberate act of petty revenge escalates the whole subplot perfectly. The economy is excellent — one sentence of admission does enormous comedic work.

jokes.text: I'm sure we can get it off. Just give me your pen. / Why? What are you gonna do? / Well, I believe I'm going to stab you repeatedly. / Not here. There are cameras everywhere.
jokes.setup: Rachel is furious Ross redrew the beard. She asks for his pen.
jokes.punchline: Rachel calmly announces she's going to 'stab him repeatedly,' then immediately revises the plan based on casino surveillance — treating violence as a logistical problem rather than a moral one.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. 'I believe I'm going to stab you repeatedly' is a great line — the formal 'I believe' preceding the violence threat is perfectly calibrated. But the punchline is 'Not here. There are cameras everywhere' — Rachel's only objection is tactical, not moral, which escalates the darkness wonderfully. High quotability.

jokes.text: None of you will live with me in my hand-shaped mansion. Except you. You can live in the thumb.
jokes.setup: Joey's friends continue to doubt the hand twin fortune.
jokes.punchline: Joey's threat is a hand-shaped mansion from which he'll exile doubters — except one person who gets the thumb unit.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and one of the best Joey lines in the series. The hand-shaped mansion is an inspired image; the specific detail of 'you can live in the thumb' — granting one person a lesser, thumb-shaped dwelling as a consolation — is perfect absurdist escalation. Joey's architectural vision of his wealth is specific, visual, and completely within character. Very high quotability. This is the kind of joke that gets quoted for decades.

jokes.text: Oh, well. / Hello, Vegas? We would like more alcohol. You know what else? We would like some more beers. / Oh, I forgot to dial.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are drunk in their hotel room playing cards, and want more drinks.
jokes.punchline: Monica 'calls' Vegas by picking up the phone and announcing their drink order to no one — she forgot to dial. The drunk logic of calling 'Vegas' as a singular entity is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Hello, Vegas?' as a phone greeting is a great drunk-logic joke. Monica calling 'Vegas' as though it's a person who delivers drinks, then forgetting to actually dial, is a good escalating drunk bit. 'We would like some more beers' as an addition to 'more alcohol' is redundant in a funny way.

jokes.text: They really overcharge you for that stuff. But who cares, because it's all on me.
jokes.setup: Ross gets a drink at the casino bar.
jokes.punchline: Chandler complains about the price, then immediately announces he's paying — the complaint made pointless by his own generosity.
jokes.explanation: Light gag. Chandler's self-undermining complaint is mild character comedy — him being both frugal and generous simultaneously. Functional but not notable.

jokes.text: Really like those macadamia nuts? / Nope.
jokes.setup: Monica has been compulsively eating expensive macadamia nuts despite their cost.
jokes.punchline: When Ross asks if she's enjoying them, Monica flatly says 'Nope' — continuing to eat them anyway, compulsive consumption divorced from enjoyment.
jokes.explanation: Monica's compulsive eating despite not enjoying the food is a great character-specific beat. 'Nope' as a monosyllabic answer while presumably still eating is very Monica — control issues playing out in reverse. Good economy.

jokes.text: And I wrote a song for us. / [sings] This hand is your hand / This hand is my hand / Oh, wait, that's your hand / No, wait, it's my hand
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to convince the dealer (his hand twin) to go into business together.
jokes.punchline: Joey has written a song for the hand twin act — a parody of a folk standard about hands that immediately loses track of whose hand is whose.
jokes.explanation: Joey's hand twin song is a great absurdist set piece. The song parodies the structure of a folk anthem while immediately undermining itself by losing track of which hand belongs to whom — which is thematically perfect (the whole premise is about identical hands being indistinguishable). Good character integration.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. I look like my great-aunt Muriel.
jokes.setup: Rachel is stuck in the hotel room with the drawn-on beard, looking in the mirror.
jokes.punchline: Of all the people Rachel could look like, she resembles her great-aunt Muriel — the specificity of 'great-aunt Muriel' (not just 'an old woman') makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'great-aunt Muriel' is what makes this land. A generic comparison to an old man would be less funny — 'Muriel' as a name is perfect, conjuring a very specific visual.

jokes.text: Thirteen. / Hit me. / Twenty-three. / Which is what we play to at this casino!
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler play homemade blackjack in their room to avoid going downstairs.
jokes.punchline: Monica busts at 23 and Chandler insists 23 is the target — making up casino rules to keep the game going and avoid admitting Monica lost.
jokes.explanation: Chandler making up casino rules to avoid his girlfriend losing — specifically inventing '23 is the target' — is sweet and absurd. Good character integration for Chandler's people-pleasing tendencies.

jokes.text: You win 10 dollars! / I bet 20. / Right.
jokes.setup: Chandler awards Monica her winnings.
jokes.punchline: Monica points out she bet 20; Chandler's flat 'Right' acknowledges he has no intention of paying correctly.
jokes.explanation: Quick joke on Chandler's casual cheating. 'Right.' is a good minimalist response that implies complete awareness and total indifference. Good economy.

jokes.text: A new pair of shoes for the Chan-Chan man!
jokes.setup: Monica is drunk and winning at their home blackjack game.
jokes.punchline: 'Chan-Chan man' as a drunk nickname for Chandler, delivered with the enthusiasm of someone who's just won the World Series.
jokes.explanation: 'Chan-Chan man' is a memorable drunk Monica nickname. The enthusiasm of her declaration is out of proportion to winning a fake blackjack game, which is funny.

jokes.text: We get the biggest suite in the place! / The biggest suite in the place!
jokes.setup: Monica's craps roll keeps winning, escalating the stakes of each roll.
jokes.punchline: Both Monica and Chandler announce the prize as if it's already won — before the roll — and then 'Come on!' — the drunk enthusiasm for a bet they're about to make.
jokes.explanation: Their shared drunk enthusiasm is charming but the joke itself is mild. Works mainly as escalation toward the marriage proposal.

jokes.text: You roll another hard eight... and we get married here tonight.
jokes.setup: Monica has been on a winning streak. Chandler has been building toward celebrating their anniversary.
jokes.punchline: Chandler proposes a drunken Vegas marriage contingent on a craps roll — the most romantic and least romantic gesture possible simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's key dramatic-comedy moments. Chandler's dice-roll marriage proposal is both a genuine romantic gesture and a ridiculous one — that tension is what makes it work. The choice to let a craps die determine marriage is perfect for a drunk anniversary in Vegas. High impact score for the room-silencing comedic surprise.

jokes.text: That's a four. / And where's the other one? / Under the table. / Nobody move! You look that way, I look this way.
jokes.setup: Monica rolled toward a marriage. One die shows four, the other has gone under the table.
jokes.punchline: Monica and Chandler's frantic search for the second die — both desperately wanting it to be a four — becomes a physical comedy set piece with assigned search quadrants.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of the die search is well-constructed. 'Nobody move' followed by assigning search quadrants ('you look that way, I look this way') is an escalation of their drunk romantic commitment. The audience is invested in the result, which makes the comedy land harder.

jokes.text: That could be 4 or 5. / It's your call.
jokes.setup: They find the missing die in an ambiguous position.
jokes.punchline: Chandler tells Monica 'it's your call' — placing the marriage decision entirely on a die she gets to interpret however she wants.
jokes.explanation: The 'it's your call' as the conclusion to a marriage proposal is a great character moment. Chandler is essentially saying 'I want to marry you but I'll let a die be your excuse either way.' The structure of an ambiguous die being the most romantic moment of the season is excellent.

jokes.text: That's it. You and me. Outside! I wouldn't want you to lose a chunk of that pretty blond hair!
jokes.setup: Phoebe has lost to the lurker old woman again at the slots.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe threatens to take the old lady 'outside' for a fight, escalating from slot machine competition to physical confrontation with a hair-pulling threat.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe threatening an old lady over slot machines is inherently funny. The specific threat of 'pretty blond hair' — implying intimate knowledge of the lady's appearance and a targeted attack — is a good detail. Phoebe's street-tough past comes through perfectly.

jokes.text: Okay, your lurking days are over. / ... / Everyone you lurk, I'll lurk first. You move on, I'll be one step ahead of you every single time. And then I'll be on your ass every hour of every day till Monday... because that's when I go home. / When do you leave? / Also Monday. / What time? Maybe we can share a cab.
jokes.setup: Phoebe delivers an intense face-off speech to the lurker old lady, threatening to out-lurk her.
jokes.punchline: The old lady asks when Phoebe leaves — the confrontation ends when they discover they share a departure day and might share a cab, completely deflating the hostility.
jokes.explanation: The best payoff of a running gag in the episode. Phoebe's intense dramatic monologue — 'I'll be on your ass every hour of every day till Monday' — is Phoebe at her funniest: deadly serious about something completely absurd. But the genius is the punchline: 'because that's when I go home' deflates the entire threat, and discovering they both leave Monday and might share a cab turns enemies into accidental travel companions in seconds. The structure of a dramatic escalation punctured by a mundane logistics question is excellent. The best-constructed joke in the episode.

jokes.text: That must be our alcohol and beers.
jokes.setup: Monica called 'Vegas' for drinks and then forgot to dial.
jokes.punchline: When there's a knock at the door, Chandler confidently assumes Vegas has delivered — despite the call never being made.
jokes.explanation: Quick callback that lands on the ongoing drunk logic. Chandler's certainty despite the failed call is the joke.

jokes.text: It's Joey! I love Joey! Oh, I love Joey! Joey lives with a duck.
jokes.setup: Joey arrives at the door. Monica and Chandler are very drunk.
jokes.punchline: Monica's drunk enthusiasm escalates from 'I love Joey!' to the seemingly random declaration 'Joey lives with a duck' — a non-sequitur that drunk Monica apparently finds deeply significant.
jokes.explanation: 'Joey lives with a duck' as drunk Monica's climactic Joey-related thought is an inspired choice. It's a true fact about Joey (he has a pet duck) made hilarious by being her brain's most important Joey data point. Great drunk character comedy.

jokes.text: Are you okay? / Yeah. Fine. Thanks.
jokes.setup: Joey has asked Monica and Chandler to help convince his hand twin to cooperate. Chandler is very drunk.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's flat 'Yeah. Fine. Thanks.' — clearly not fine — delivered in drunk near-monosyllables is a good reaction beat.
jokes.explanation: Mild reaction beat. Gets a small laugh from Chandler's obvious not-okayness. Not particularly crafted but functional.

jokes.text: Hey, Rach? How you doing? / I'm doing good, baby. How you doing?
jokes.setup: Joey checks on a drunk Rachel.
jokes.punchline: Rachel responds to Joey's signature 'How you doing?' with her own 'How you doing?' — she's so drunk she's absorbed his catchphrase and his 'baby' affectation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best drunk jokes. Rachel has absorbed Joey's exact phrasing, including 'baby,' and fires it back at him. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a catchphrase callback, it characterizes drunk Rachel perfectly, and Joey's presumably confused/flattered reaction adds visual comedy. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Don't let her drink anymore.
jokes.setup: Drunk Rachel does Joey's catchphrase back at him.
jokes.punchline: Joey's flat instruction to Chandler — 'don't let her drink anymore' — implies this is the worst possible outcome of his catchphrase being used.
jokes.explanation: Joey's concern is funny because it's not 'is she okay?' but 'stop her from doing my thing.' Good button on the catchphrase joke.

jokes.text: Here's that macadamia nut. / No, something else.
jokes.setup: Earlier, Monica was shown marveling at an expensive macadamia nut. Now Chandler offers her one.
jokes.punchline: Monica, in her drunken state, now rejects the macadamia nut — having forgotten her earlier enthusiasm or wanting something else entirely.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the macadamia nut moment. Mildly funny as a character beat — drunk Monica has changed her preferences.

jokes.text: Okay, you know what? There is only one way I am leaving this hotel room. / Well, hello! I'm Ross.
jokes.setup: Rachel refuses to leave the room because of her drawn-on beard. Ross has a solution.
jokes.punchline: Ross appears in matching drawn-on facial hair — giving Rachel a companion rather than removing the problem. 'Well, hello! I'm Ross.' is delivered as if meeting her at a party.
jokes.explanation: Ross's solution to Rachel's beard problem — getting his own — is a sweet and funny character move. His formal introduction of himself as 'Ross' as though they've just met adds the right absurdist layer. The visual of them both with drawn-on beards is a strong sight gag.

jokes.text: I won! I won! I finally won! I won! That was my quarter! / Take a hike, toots.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been pursuing the lurker old woman across the casino floor.
jokes.punchline: The old woman wins on Phoebe's machine — and when Phoebe confronts her, the lady calls her 'toots' and dismisses her, flipping the predator/prey dynamic.
jokes.explanation: 'Take a hike, toots' from the old lady is a great line — she has zero remorse and treats Phoebe as the nuisance. The reversal of Phoebe hunting the lurker only to be dismissed as 'toots' is good situational irony.

jokes.text: Excuse me, sir. This lady played my quarter. / Is that true, miss? / Sells drugs to kids.
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls security to dispute the jackpot. The guard asks the old lady if she played Phoebe's quarter.
jokes.punchline: The old lady responds to a question about slot machines by accusing Phoebe of selling drugs to children — a completely nuclear, unrelated escalation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The old lady's response to being caught — immediately accusing Phoebe of selling drugs to kids — is a perfect dark escalation. The specificity of 'to kids' makes it funnier than a generic accusation. The gap between the question (did you use her quarter?) and the answer (she sells drugs to children) is maximally large, which is what makes it work. Great economy — three words do enormous comedic damage. High quotability.

jokes.text: I won't go back to that hellhole!
jokes.setup: Security is escorting Phoebe out after the drug accusation.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's melodramatic cry of 'I won't go back to that hellhole!' implies a prior criminal history with the casino — treating being removed from a Vegas casino as though she's being sent back to prison.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's past life on the streets makes this line work on multiple levels — it's not entirely impossible she means it. The escalation of a slot machine dispute to Phoebe treating casino ejection as reincarceration is excellent absurdist character comedy. 'Hellhole' is a funny word choice for a Las Vegas casino.

jokes.text: I need something old, something new, something borrowed and something blue. / Here's something blue and new. / You are so efficient. I love you.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are very drunk and apparently deciding to get married.
jokes.punchline: Chandler produces something blue and new immediately, and Monica compliments his efficiency as if he's done excellent project management rather than enabled an impulsive Vegas marriage.
jokes.explanation: Monica's 'you are so efficient, I love you' in response to Chandler producing a wedding necessity is funny because it's such a Monica response — even drunk wedding planning requires organized execution. Good character integration.

jokes.text: We need something old. / I have a condom in my wallet that I've had since I was twelve. / That'll work. / I don't think so.
jokes.setup: They need 'something old' for the wedding. Chandler offers a solution.
jokes.punchline: Chandler has had a condom in his wallet since age twelve — implying decades of optimistic preparedness that was apparently never needed. Joey agrees it qualifies; Monica disagrees.
jokes.explanation: Very funny Chandler character joke. The implication that the condom has been there since age twelve — both pathetic in its optimism and funny in its specificity — is a great reveal. Joey immediately approving it as 'something old' while Monica is horrified is a perfect character dynamic. High quotability and character integration.

jokes.text: Now something borrowed. / Here, just take this. / That's stealing. / We'll bring it back. Put it under your dress.
jokes.setup: They need 'something borrowed' for the wedding. Joey immediately produces an item.
jokes.punchline: Joey hands over something he intends for her to stuff under her dress — implying he's taken (stolen) it from somewhere in the casino. 'That's stealing / We'll bring it back' plays the crime with cheerful dismissal.
jokes.explanation: Joey's casual theft-as-borrowing is a good character beat. 'Put it under your dress' adds an absurd physicality. The drunk wedding logistics are inherently funny.

jokes.text: My name is Regina Falangie. I'm a businesswoman in town on business. Would you like to see my card? What did I do with my Filofax? I must've left it in Conference Room B.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been thrown out of the casino but re-enters in disguise. She needs to pass as a different person.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's alter ego 'Regina Falangie' is a businesswoman whose persona immediately falls apart — she can't find her business card and has left her Filofax in 'Conference Room B' (a room that doesn't exist in a casino).
jokes.explanation: Regina Falangie is a great character invention. The name, the instantly failing cover story, and the absurd 'Conference Room B' detail make this one of Phoebe's best bits. 'I must've left it in Conference Room B' is the kind of specific wrong detail that makes an absurdist bit land — there is no Conference Room B in a casino, which makes the false memory funnier. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Stop it. / Miss Falangie, may I ask you a question as an impartial person at this table? / Please stop it.
jokes.setup: Phoebe's fake identity is transparently obvious. Joey tries to use 'Regina Falangie' as an impartial witness for the hand twin pitch.
jokes.punchline: The dealer's repeated 'Stop it' / 'Please stop it' — identical, increasingly weary — is a great deadpan reaction to Phoebe and Joey's combined nonsense.
jokes.explanation: The dealer's escalating exhaustion expressed only through 'stop it / please stop it' is excellent economy. The 'please' in the second one implies the first request failed, adding layers of desperation. Perfect straight-man work.

jokes.text: Wouldn't you pay good money to see identical hands showcased in some type of an entertainment venue? / If you leave now, I will chop off my hand and give it to you!
jokes.setup: Joey uses Regina Falangie to pitch the hand twin to the dealer.
jokes.punchline: The dealer — pushed to his limit — offers to chop off his own hand and give it to Joey as a faster resolution than continued pitch exposure.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The dealer's threat to self-amputate is a spectacular escalation — his breaking point is so extreme it becomes dark comedy. 'If you leave now, I will chop off my hand and give it to you' is the perfect expression of someone who wants a situation to end at any cost. Dark, specific, well-structured, and very quotable.

jokes.text: Didn't I just throw you out? / No, you threw out Phoebe. I'm Regina Falangie. Falangie.
jokes.setup: Security recognizes Phoebe despite her 'disguise.'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe insists on the distinction — 'you threw out Phoebe, I'm Regina Falangie' — repeating 'Falangie' as though the surname will seal the deception.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's commitment to the obviously failed alias is great character comedy. The repetition of 'Falangie' as though it's a magic word is perfect Phoebe logic. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Come on, man. Come on, buddy. Don't let him do this. Come on! I'm your hand twin!
jokes.setup: Security is ejecting both Phoebe and Joey from the casino.
jokes.punchline: Joey's final plea — 'I'm your hand twin!' — delivered as though it grants him some protected status, is the perfect final collapse of the hand twin enterprise.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the hand twin subplot. 'I'm your hand twin!' as a final plea — as if it creates a legal or moral obligation — is a great absurdist character moment. The desperation of appealing to their hand relationship as security drags him away is exactly right. High quotability.

jokes.text: What are you doing? / The 'Wedding March.' Does that freak you out? / No, it's the graduation song.
jokes.setup: While waiting in the chapel, Chandler hums something.
jokes.punchline: Monica corrects Chandler — he's humming 'Pomp and Circumstance' (graduation) rather than the Wedding March — which either means he's confused or unconsciously expressing doubt.
jokes.explanation: Good character joke with an undertone — Chandler humming the wrong song could be nerves, confusion, or Freudian. The easy response of 'it's the graduation song' rather than any other correction is funny in its matter-of-fact delivery. Monica not making it a big deal is the right choice.

jokes.text: Hello, Mrs. Ross! / Well, hello, Mr. Rachel!
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are waiting to get married and greet each other playfully.
jokes.punchline: They exchange name-swap greetings — 'Mrs. Ross' and 'Mr. Rachel' — getting each other's potential married names wrong in a way that highlights how unusual their situation is.
jokes.explanation: A cute joke that works because of the swap — 'Mrs. Ross' implies Chandler is taking her last name, 'Mr. Rachel' inverts names entirely. The drunk logic of calling each other by the wrong partner's name as an anniversary joke is sweet and funny.

tmdb_overview:
Chandler decides the only way to mend his friendship with Joey is to fly out to Vegas and visit him. Phoebe is determined not to be left out on another adventure, so everyone winds up going. Trouble is in the water, however, when Chandler finds out that Monica had lunch with Richard. Meanwhile, Ross and Rachel try to embarrass each other after an awkward encounter.

Chandler and Monica reconcile and hastily decide to get married. Ross and Rachel get drunk and roam the casino. Phoebe deals with a 'lurker' on the slot machines.
insight: Vegas chaos escalates to a 73-point climax fueled by character comedy and deadpan timing.
